CoreWeave Brings AI’s Financing Concern Into Focus
 
Plus, Nvidia’s spy-scandal storm rages, and corporate America braces for investigations
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Oil prices are falling this morning after President Trump signaled that further strikes on Iran aren’t likely at the moment. That is helping Dow futures as stock investors assess yesterday’s broad rally. Treasury yields are higher before this morning’s October inflation report, the last reading on consumer prices ahead of the Fed’s December meeting. Play ball

 

When it comes to AI, the market is contemplating a reverse “Field of Dreams” scenario. 

 

AI companies already see enormous demand from corporations and consumers marching toward them. The question is whether they will be able to build the capacity to meet that demand.

 

And, crucially, whether they will be able to finance that build-out without driving up the cost of subscriptions or tokens. Higher pricing for AI could discourage the rapid adoption of it for business, science or shopping. And that could put even more pressure on the valuation multiples of companies priced for hypergrowth.

 

Just how pressing this financing concern is may become more apparent this week. Two companies whose fates are linked to the cost of building out computing power report earnings: CoreWeave on Tuesday after the bell and Amsterdam-based Nebius Group on Thursday.

 

These companies compete with the likes of “hyperscale” giants Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft in the business of hosting computing in the cloud. But they are far younger, and rely more heavily on debt to finance the chips and data centers they will need to keep growing. They are sometimes referred to as “neoclouds.”

 

Their role in the AI ecosystem is important. While they sell computing power, neoclouds aren’t promoting their own AI models. This makes them independent partners for hyperscalers and the likes of Anthropic or OpenAI.

 

Few investors were focused on CoreWeave until a few weeks ago, when its high-yield “junk” bonds plunged in price, sending yields soaring. On Monday, CoreWeave’s most actively traded issue, a 9.625% bond that matures in 2032, was yielding around 15%, according to MarketAxess data. Its shares have fallen about 40% over the past month.

 

That’s bad news if 15% is the prevailing cost of new debt for anyone other than hyperscale giants. Plans to acquire chips and build data centers may become economically unfeasible.

 

There are ways to work around this, and the market will be listening for such plans. For starters, higher yields on already-issued debt are a warning about future financing, but not about the company’s current financing costs.

 

And the neoclouds have another option. Although unsecured junk bonds have been hammered, the pricing on many secured loans and bonds has fared far better. Those debts are backed either by the data centers themselves, or by contracts to sell that computing to a giant such as Meta. 

 

So that funding route remains open. Now, CoreWeave and others must convince investors they can minimize the use of expensive debt while still delivering the computing power everyone is coming for.

↗️ Nvidia: Shares of the chip giant ticked up premarket after yesterday’s slide, as investors continue to digest the impact of an investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was a spying target of China.

 

↘️ Rocket Lab: The space company posted a jump in revenue, but its loss widened more than analysts had expected. Its stock slid premarket.

 

↘️ Vodafone: Shares of the U.K. telecommunications group edged down after it raised its full-year guidance but called out weakness in its German business.

Nvidia’s Chinese spy scandal might curb some of the more cavalier instincts of the company and its AI rock star chief executive, Jensen Huang. That wouldn’t ultimately be such a bad thing for Nvidia and its investors.
